b0162f8d78377040: HAZLE TOWNSHIP: On his terrace overlooking the forest in eastern Pennsylvania, Ed Negra lays out four letters. All are from a developer promising a US$10,000 check to each household once its data centre is running.
"I call it a bribe," says the American retiree.
The scene is picture-perfect. Autumn leaves are turning russet, and there is a stunning mountain view in this corner of Pennsylvania, a key state in America's upcoming midterm elections.
"We thought it was a beautiful place to retire," says the septuagenarian, who used to manage a large building-supply store in neighbouring New Jersey.
He and his wife settled in a sprawling gated community with round-the-clock security.
Eagle Rock Resort, in Hazle Township, has hundreds of comfortable homes scattered through the woods, two golf courses, swimming pools, an equestrian centre and even a few ski slopes for the winter.
"We didn't know until we heard all the noise" of chainsaws in late 2024, Negra recalls.
More than 1,200 acres (500 hectares) of land below the resort were cleared to build the future server complex.
Residents quickly mobilised. They were furious that no one had warned them, and they worried about noise and pollution.
Their fight echoes many conflicts across the United States over data centres, which have become an issue in the Nov 3 vote.
Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data centre projects in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, which tracks resistance to the industry.
And polls show that the hostility crosses party lines.
But Republican president Donald Trump fervently backs these projects in the name of US dominance in artificial intelligence, and he chastises those who oppose them.
'Drop in the bucket'
In Hazle Township, residents won a court-ordered halt to construction as well as a municipal moratorium.
A few pieces of heavy equipment sit idle on the vast cleared tract. The logs have already been hauled away.
But developer NorthPoint Development has not given up.
Its letters now flood local mailboxes, saying "there is a lot of misinformation and fear that has circulated about data centres and our project."
The letters also lay out a US$165 million fund for the township and its residents.
The money would pay for a new police station, lower trash fees and more.
Part of it, US$45 million, is to be paid directly to the 4,500 households once the data centre's first building goes into service.
In the former mining town, one in six residents lives below the poverty line, according to official data.
"For a young, struggling couple... living from paycheck to paycheck, US$10,000 is a lot of money," says Jeff Fasnacht, a retired high school teacher who lives in the gated community.
Like Negra, he sees the offer as a bribe. He also calls it "a drop in the bucket" compared with how much value his home could lose if the project goes ahead.
"This was supposed to be pristine forest forever," sighs the golf enthusiast.
Neither the developer nor township officials responded to AFP's requests for comment.
'David and Goliath'
Across the valley, residents of rural Sugarloaf Township are fighting a high-voltage power line that is likely intended to supply the data centre.
They are not eligible for the possible US$10,000 check.
"There's no amount of money that can replace or take away the beauty, the tranquility that we live in," says Annie Vinatieri. She shares a house with her in-laws, her husband and their young son.
She has been fighting the power line for almost two years.
"This fight feels akin to a David and Goliath fight," she says. She takes heart in how many residents have rallied against tech interests: "The empowerment is unbelievable."
Erika Cook, 42, lives nearby and works remotely for an insurance company.
She and her husband raise a few chickens and keep a vegetable garden. They also tap maple trees for syrup in the woods on their property.
Part of that land is now the target of an eminent domain proceeding to make room for a huge transmission tower.
Republicans dominate at the ballot box in this region. Cook says opposition to data centers has one virtue here: "It's bringing people together... across party lines."

09da524f1aaecbdd: PARIS, Oct 19 — One year after a stunning break-in at the Louvre Museum, the four main suspects are in jail awaiting trial, but police appear to have run out of leads to locate the stolen crown jewels.

Thieves disguised as workmen sliced their way into the museum with industrial disc-cutters on October 19 last year before making off with eight irreplaceable items worth an estimated US$100 million (RM408 million).
They include a brooch and crown from Napoleon III’s wife Eugenie. President Emmanuel Macron referred to the robbery as an attack on France’s history.

Experts from law enforcement and private art theft agencies who spoke to AFP believe the best chance of recovering the treasures is if the thieves acted alone and stashed their loot somewhere in the Paris region.
“There was a short period of time where they may have hidden them in a wall or buried them,” Christopher Marinello from Art Recovery International, a private agency, told AFP.
All four men were arrested within 10 days of the heist.
Interrogation
The last known sighting of the glittering 19th-century gems was on CCTV footage recorded in an underground lock-up in the gritty Aubervilliers suburb of northern Paris, where all the suspects live.
Extensive searches directed by the 100-strong investigation team have been carried out at their homes and families’ homes, in cellars, garages and attics — all to no avail.

If the jewels have been hidden or handed to a “fence” for safekeeping, there is still a chance that one of the suspects confesses in exchange for a more lenient sentence, said renowned Dutch private art detective Arthur Brand.
“The French police are very professional, they know how to interrogate, they know how to put pressure on (someone),” he told AFP.
“You only need one to talk, and in many cases, one talks.”
Dismantling

The more worrying scenario is that the gang was acting on orders from a ringleader or middleman with links to organised crime — to whom they handed the jewels once they had finished their smash-and-grab.

“The power of organised crime is not only to bring the experience to commit a crime, but also to have people to take the objects and sell them,” said Corrado Catesi, head of the stolen art unit at international police body Interpol.
In custody, two of the suspects have claimed a ringleader was part of their team, which is being treated with scepticism by investigators, a source close to the case told AFP recently.
The worst-case scenario is that the jewels were transported either out of France or to a local contact in the underground precious stones business.
“It’s mainly diamonds, so they have to dismantle them, recut them and sell them. If they would go to one place, it would be Antwerp,” said Brand, referring to the Belgian diamond hub.
Marinello lists Tel Aviv and India as other possible destinations.

Tobias Kormind, managing director of 77 Diamonds, Europe’s largest online diamond jeweller, told AFP that “once recut, re-entering the legitimate supply chain to be bought by wholesalers or retailers is fairly straightforward”.
“Unless a stone possessed ultra-distinctive internal inclusions, even top diamond laboratories like the GIA would struggle to flag a freshly polished diamond as stolen property,” he said.
‘Still a chance’
But if the jewels fell into the hands of an organised crime group, there appears to be still some grounds for hope.

Brand referred to several cases where stolen jewels were recovered, notably after a raid on the TEFAF art fair in the Netherlands in 2022 or the break-in at the Grünes Gewölbe museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2019.
“Although we all think that most of the gold, silver and diamonds that get stolen, we never see them back, in some cases, we do,” he explained.
“There is still a chance that we will see the Louvre jewels again and it might be that somebody talks before the court case.”
The jewels remain listed as missing in Interpol’s database of stolen artworks.
Analysis of investigations around the world reveals that objects “can take from three months to 40 years to be recovered”, Catesi told AFP. — AFP
dda1cf8ce9a0159a: KUALA LUMPUR: Kerajaan dan beberapa pegawai polis memohon Mahkamah Tinggi memutuskan lima persoalan undang-undang melibatkan saman kecuaian difailkan anak lelaki Anna Jenkins, yang rangka mayat ibunya ditemui di tapak pembinaan di Pulau Pinang pada 2020.

Greg Jenkins menuntut ganti rugi daripada polis, pihak berkuasa kerajaan, dan pihak lain, serta perintah mahkamah untuk memaksa pihak berkuasa membuka semula siasatan terhadap kematian ibunya sebagai kes disyaki bunuh.

Dia memfailkan saman itu pada Ogos 2023, dengan peringkat awal menamakan kerajaan, polis, Berjaya Land Development Sdn Bhd, pengurus projeknya Terrence Theseira, dan pekerja landskap Kew Kee Seng sebagai defendan.

Seorang daripada pegawai polis, Azrul Azizan Mat Rawi yang dinamakan sebagai defendan mengesahkan afidavit bagi menyokong permohonan defendan keempat hingga kelapan.
Defendan bergantung kepada Aturan 14A dan Aturan 33 Kaedah-kaedah Mahkamah 2012 untuk memohon penentuan persoalan undang-undang berkenaan sebelum perbicaraan penuh berjalan.

Mahkamah juga diminta menentukan sama ada kegagalan didakwa itu boleh menyokong tuntutan salah laku, salah guna, atau peninggalan kewajipan dalam jawatan awam.

Persoalan lain adalah sama ada kegagalan mengesan orang hilang, menentukan punca kematian, atau mengenal pasti suspek sudah memadai membuktikan hubungan sebab dan akibat yang diperlukan bagi tuntutan ganti rugi.
e92c3f0c029f8b88: KUALA LUMPUR: Pakatan Harapan (PH) belum membincangkan pemilihan ‘poster boy’ bagi PRN Melaka pada 14 Nov ini, termasuk cadangan menamakan Adly Zahari.

1219ded2ccd25a3b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — The Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) has been disqualified from the South-east Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), costing it its turn at the forum’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

SEANF said in a statement today that its Governing Board found the MNHRC no longer met the forum’s definition of a national human rights institution, following a formal review of its eligibility that began on Aug 14.
The board passed the resolution on Oct 1, with immediate effect.

The decision was reached by consensus among the chairpersons of five member institutions: Indonesia’s National Commission of Human Rights (Komnas HAM), the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam), the Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines (CHRP), the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand (NHRCT) and Timor-Leste’s Ombudsman for Human Rights and Justice (PDHJ).
As a result, the MNHRC can no longer take part in SEANF’s 23rd Annual Conference this year or any other SEANF meetings.
According to the statement, the MNHRC was notified in writing on Sept 1 and given the opportunity to respond. It was also invited to the Oct 1 board meeting at which the resolution was considered.
The Myanmar commission replied through a letter dated Sept 24 and a press statement issued on Sept 26, saying it rejected and disassociated itself from the review.
The board said the responses did not satisfactorily address the matters raised in the notice.

Under the amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure, a national human rights institution is defined as “an independent national institution that complies with the Paris Principles and holds a constitutional and/or legislative mandate to promote and protect human rights”.
SEANF said the MNHRC is free to reapply for membership once it can demonstrate discernible efforts towards compliance with the Paris Principles, as provided under Article 6(3) of the rules.

The forum stressed that the decision was made in a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner, in line with its rules and guided by the procedural best practices of the Asia Pacific Forum of National Human Rights Institutions (APF).

It added that, as “A” status-accredited institutions, SEANF members share a collective responsibility to uphold the forum’s credibility, integrity and accountability, and to promote and protect human rights across the region in line with the Paris Principles.
cb8f8e9234a67cb5: PETALING JAYA: Two Umno leaders have poured cold water on Wawasan’s desire to contest the Sungai Udang and Bemban state seats in the Melaka election, citing Perikatan Nasional’s (PN) current circumstance as well as the coalition’s narrow victories in both constituencies.
Umno Supreme Council member Nur Jazlan Mohamed said the party should only negotiate with PAS regarding the distribution of seats, given PN's suspension by the Registrar of Societies.
"It would be more appropriate and fair for Wawasan’s seat demands to be settled internally within PN, rather than by pressuring Umno, which leads Barisan Nasional (BN).
"BN should only negotiate with PAS, as the issue of PN’s status has yet to be resolved with the RoS," he told FMT.
Yesterday, Wawasan president Hamzah Zainudin said the party wanted to defend the Sungai Udang and Bemban seats in the Melaka polls, just as Umno intended to defend the 21 seats it previously held.

Hamzah said Wawasan had the right to contest the seats according to the principle of incumbency.
He also said any negotiations must take into account the interests of all parties, and Wawasan’s demands should not be sidelined simply because others are also interested in contesting the seats.

KTMB said its auxiliary police will intensify patrols and security monitoring to safeguard rail infrastructure and ensure smooth train operations.

5cd1ef9d085b529d: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that his administration would begin renovation work next month on a historic Washington golf course that a federal judge had ordered could not proceed without prior court notification.
The renovation work, which Trump earlier this year had said would begin in September, has become the subject of a lawsuit over environmental and historic preservation concerns.

Trump wrote in a Sunday morning post on Truth Social that work on the East Potomac Golf Links would begin on November 15 and that it would reopen in about 15 months. Trump later posted that the Interior Department, which oversees the golf course, "is very excited" about the latest renovation plans.
The renovation is among a number of projects Trump is pursuing to reshape the White House and other Washington landmarks.

US District Judge Ana Reyes ruled earlier this year that the government must give notice before any substantive construction work on the golf course could proceed, and last week issued an order halting the removal of trees at the site, which she called "inexcusable."

After the president's posts appeared on Truth Social, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to explain whether it maintained its position argued last week that there is "no final agency action" regarding the course, and that at most, "the President has given preliminary thought" to the renovations.
Responding to the judge's order, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a filing that any redesign of the golf course is not an "agency action."

"Just as a decision to redesign all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum would not be agency action, neither would a decision to redesign a golf course, or to trim trees, replace fences, expand the fairways, or mow the lawn," Woodward wrote.

The DC Preservation League brought a lawsuit in February to halt the administration's takeover of the golf course, alleging that it would violate ⁠environmental laws and "irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history."
In an October 9 court filing, the Trump administration had asked Reyes to dismiss the litigation, saying it was premature ​because the "proposed project remains ⁠at an early and conceptual stage."

The following day, however, the government removed about 500 trees from the site, which it said would improve safety at the park ​and restore its original design, and was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump's ambitions for the course. Reyes ordered a halt to the removals.

On Friday, the government filed a motion to disqualify Reyes and move the case to another district judge, saying her actions had shown "deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy toward the Trump Administration," according to court records.
ebd12fab9d5807e7: SINGAPORE: Indonesian stocks slid to a six-year low on Monday as a warning from MSCI over possible expulsion from its global indexes next year rattled fragile investor sentiment, sharpening the focus on how Jakarta intends to allay the index provider's concerns.

Jakarta's benchmark stocks fell over 5% in early trading on Monday after plunging 11.6% on Friday, as the world's worst performers reeled from index provider MSCI saying it was considering shifting Indonesia to "standalone" status from its current "emerging markets" mantle.

A shift to standalone status would risk cutting Southeast Asia's biggest economy off from international capital, relegate it to an investment backwater and club it with a group of standalone markets that includes Lebanon and Zimbabwe.
The more-severe-than-expected move has raised the stakes for Indonesia's regulators and finance officials.

On Monday, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it cut its lower auto-rejection limit to 7% from 15% to give investors "an opportunity to evaluate and digest available information, helping them make better investment decisions based on Indonesia's economic fundamentals".
The move followed a weekend meeting between the financial regulator and capital market participants, including analysts and economists.

An Indonesian regulator on Friday also unveiled sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms, with the fines totalling 2.1 trillion rupiah (US$116.4 million).

Angus Mackintosh, an Asean specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the fact the fines were announced on Friday suggests that Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) has been working on the matter for a while.

"The fines are a positive move, but there needs to be concerted action to stamp the authority of the OJK and take direct action against certain well-known players who have been involved in market abuse," he said.

MSCI had threatened a downgrade to "frontier" status in January because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour but said on Friday the lack of progress in remedying those concerns meant even a drop to that status would not reflect the severity of the issues.

"The burden of proof has shifted: avoiding reclassification will require clear evidence that the announced reforms have been consistently implemented and materially improved market functioning," strategists at Goldman Sachs said in a note.

Goldman Sachs estimates a full MSCI removal could trigger US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. Active funds benchmarked to these indexes hold more than US$8 billion, although any selling would be discretionary rather than benchmark-driven, they wrote.
Foreign investors have net sold US$4.88 billion worth of Indonesian stocks so far this year, on track for the biggest annual outflow in at least 16 years.
Aninda Mitra, head of Asia macro and investment strategy at BNY Investments, said foreign equity exposure to Indonesia has shrunk to the point where "there may not be much more downside from here."
"But at the same time, even if there are some interesting and fundamentally sound companies and banks, attracting sufficiently large amounts of capital will be tougher in this environment," he said.

MSCI's warning raises the stakes for the government of president Prabowo Subianto, which has faced a series of setbacks this year, with Moody's and Fitch having cut their sovereign rating outlooks to negative earlier in 2026.
Investors are also fretting over the ramifications beyond the US$500 billion stock market, with the rupiah weakening to 18,040 per dollar, not far from the record low of 18,190 hit in June.

"Our bigger concern is not index-related selling itself," said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore, "but the potential near-term spillover into the rupiah and domestic bond yields, where market dislocation could translate into tighter financial conditions and a more meaningful impact on the real economy."
42ab126ae63ca942: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, today received the credentials of 18 foreign heads of mission to Malaysia at Istana Negara here.
The presentation of credentials ceremony was held at the Singgahsana Kecil of the palace.

The foreign heads of mission were Spanish Ambassador Sergio Farré Salva, Namibian High Commissioner Christine Hoebes, Belgian Ambassador Peter Huyghebaert and South African High Commissioner Maud Vuyelwa Dlomo.

Also presenting their credentials were Azerbaijani Ambassador Khazar Farhadov, Iraqi Ambassador Adnan Mhalhal Azara Al Maajoon, Indian High Commissioner Somnath Ghosh, Dutch Ambassador Michel Leon Hans Deelen and Omani Ambassador Hatim Hilal Ali Al Yaqoubi.

The other representatives were Chum Angvichet of Cambodia, Malik Kenesbayuly Murzalin of Kazakhstan, Pham Thi Thuy Nga of Vietnam, Major-General Mbaraka Naziad Mkeremy of Tanzania, José Julio Gómez Beato of the Dominican Republic, Dharamkumar Seeraj of Guyana, Maria Camilleri of Malta, Dimitrios Michalopoulos of Greece and Nicholas Panayiotou of Cyprus.
Meanwhile, Sultan Ibrahim also presented letters of appointment to three newly appointed Malaysian heads of mission to foreign countries.
They were Malaysian High Commissioner to Canada John K. Samuel, Malaysian Ambassador to Belgium Shaiful Anuar Mohammad and Malaysian Ambassador to Iran Datuk Wan Aznainizam Yusri Wan Abdul Rashid.

Also present at the ceremony were Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan, Istana Negara Comptroller of the Royal Household Tan Sri Dr Azmi Rohani and Foreign Ministry Deputy Secretary-General (Bilateral Affairs) Datuk Syed Mohamad Hasrin Tengku Hussin. — Bernama
3dc224cb223b6d84: KUALA LUMPUR: The government and several police officers are seeking a High Court ruling on five legal questions before a negligence suit brought by the son of Anna Jenkins, whose remains were found at a Penang construction site in 2020, proceeds to trial.

Greg Jenkins is seeking damages from the police, government authorities and other parties, as well as a court order compelling the authorities to reopen the investigation into his mother’s death as a suspected murder case.
He filed the suit in August 2023, initially naming the government, police, Berjaya Land Development Sdn Bhd, its project manager Terrence Theseira, and landscape worker Kew Kee Seng as defendants.
However, on Sept 25, 2025, the Court of Appeal upheld a ruling striking out Berjaya Land and Theseira from the negligence suit.
The latest application seeks an early determination of five questions of law that the remaining defendants say could resolve or narrow the issues in dispute.
Azrul Azizan Mat Rawi, one of the police officers named as a defendant, has affirmed an affidavit supporting the application by the fourth to eighth defendants.
The defendants are relying on Orders 14A and 33 of the Rules of Court 2012 to seek a determination of the legal questions before a full trial.

One of the questions is whether the police owe a duty of care to a missing person or her family when investigating a disappearance, and whether an allegedly inadequate investigation can give rise to claims of negligence or breach of statutory duty.
The court has also been asked to determine whether the alleged failures could support claims of misfeasance, malfeasance or nonfeasance in public office.

Another question is whether the failure to locate a missing person, establish the cause of death or identify a suspected perpetrator is sufficient to establish the causal link required for a claim for damages.
7434b3193e34c3e3: SAO PAULO: Firing off personal attacks, Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro held an acrimonious first debate Sunday, a week before a tight presidential election runoff.

A chaotic exchange between the two men, who called each other liars on multiple occasions, accusing each other of corruption and dragging up various scandals, encapsulated the tone of a bitter election campaign in the deeply polarised nation.
Bolsonaro, 45, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, secured a shock first-round lead over Lula earlier this month, and polls predict a close battle for the runoff on Oct 25.
The two men sparred over the economy, public security, healthcare, corruption, and Brazil's ties to the US.

"Brazil is going to retire you," fired off Bolsonaro, seeking to unnerve his adversary by pacing up and down behind him throughout the debate in view of the camera, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing while his adversary spoke.
Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug" and said he did not want to stand close to a "militiaman", alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups.
Bolsonaro, who made several jabs about Lula's time jailed for corruption on charges that were later annulled, retorted that it was better he stay at a distance "because my wallet could be stolen."
Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in power, battled to control his irritation at times and repeatedly asked viewers to "look it up on Google" to prove his adversary was lying.
While Bolsonaro has led in polls since the first round, his edge slightly narrowed in two polls this week, which showed him with 51% of voting intentions compared to 49% for Lula.
'Subservient' to US interests

Bolsonaro hammered away at the primary concerns of Brazilians – such as the cost of living and insecurity – and accused Lula of "reckless spending to get re-elected" due to various social measures he has announced while campaigning.

Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic "chainsaw" cuts to public spending implemented by Argentina's libertarian President Javier Milei, which led to higher unemployment and cuts to benefits.
Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro dodged the question and pivoted to different topics.
Lula questioned the right winger's ties to US President Donald Trump – an ally of the Bolsonaro family – and plans to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals.
"It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula.
Former president Jair Bolsonaro came up several times, including when his son asked Lula why so many prisoners had supported him in the election.
Lula said he wanted all of their votes, including that of Jair Bolsonaro – who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for a botched coup bid after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
"Vote for me, Bolsonaro, you know your son, you know I'm better than him."
'A state of calamity'
Ahead of the showdown, tens of thousands of supporters of Lula and Bolsonaro gathered in cities around the country.
In Sao Paulo, a sea of people dressed in the yellow and green of the Brazilian flag rallied for Flavio Bolsonaro, who made his way down Paulista Avenue on the back of a truck.

"The country is in a state of calamity. To make ends meet or buy anything, you have to work two or three jobs just to pay the bills," said Sara Machado, 36, wearing a T-shirt with the slogan "Right-wing. With pride."
The rally drew about 71,000 people, according to monitors at the University of Sao Paulo (USP).
Swimmers and singers for Lula
In Rio de Janeiro, swimmers at Praia Vermelha beach synchronised in the water to spell out Lula's name with their bodies.
Later, on Copacabana Beach, iconic octogenarian singer Caetano Veloso led a "rally for democracy" in favour of the president, which USP monitors said drew some 56,000 people.

Fabiana Leite, a 51-year-old nurse and social worker, said Lula's social welfare programmes saved her after she was wrongly incarcerated, lost custody of her daughters, and had to rebuild her life after being freed.
"You might have the desire to fight and to grow, but without the means, without social programmes, it's just not possible. That is why I am here, continuing the fight," she told AFP.
b66063439655a72d: KLANG: Pempengaruh politik Wan Azri Wan Deris dilepas dan dibebaskan oleh Mahkamah Sesyen di sini daripada pertuduhan membuat kenyataan berbaur hasutan terhadap kerajaan.
Hakim Siti Aminah Ghazali dalam keputusan ringkasnya memutuskan pihak pendakwaan gagal membuktikan pertuduhan terhadap Azri mengikut Seksyen 4(1) Akta Hasutan melampaui keraguan munasabah.
Mahkamah turut memerintahkan wang jaminannya berjumlah RM7,000 dikembalikan.
Wan Azri didakwa membuat kenyataan bahawa kerajaan 'pro-Israel dan pro-Barat' menerusi akaun Facebook 'Halid Hamidi (Halid Mat Kool)' kira-kira 1 tengah hari pada 8 Nov 2023.
Wan Azri diwakili peguam Rafique Rashid Ali, manakala Timbalan Pendakwa Raya Mustaffa P Kunyalam dan Nadia Izhar hadir bagi pihak pendakwaan.
Dia pada mulanya dibebaskan oleh Mahkamah Sesyen tahun lalu, namun Mahkamah Tinggi mengarahkannya membela diri tahun ini susulan rayuan pihak pendakwaan.
8d7639e765b1657c: LOS ANGELES, Oct 18 — Paramount’s action film Street Fighter karate-chopped the competition this weekend with a US$31 million (RM130.6 million) debut at the North American box office, industry estimates showed Sunday.

However, a buzzy three-hour documentary about tech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes stole the spotlight in Hollywood after a stunning US$15 million (RM63.2 million) debut on fewer than 1,000 screens across the United States and Canada.
Street Fighter, based on the beloved Capcom video game, follows super-powered martial artists competing in a global tournament who uncover and battle a sinister conspiracy.

Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo and Callina Liang star in the film, the third feature-length adaptation of the video game and the first since production company Legendary acquired the movie rights in 2023.
Jason Momoa and Curtis Jackson, better known as rapper 50 Cent, also make appearances.
Analyst David A. Gross of Franchise Entertainment Research called the US$31 million (RM130.6 million) debut a “good opening” but noted that “critics’ reviews are weak and the audience score is soft”.
“The film should recover its costs after playing in ancillary markets, in addition to adding value back to the franchise in all its forms — in film, TV and games,” he added.
In second place was A24’s hotly anticipated documentary You Can See Everything, co-directed by comedian Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

The film follows Holmes at her home in 2023 during the month before she began an 11-year prison sentence, taking in US$15 million (RM63.2 million) on just 855 screens, according to Exhibitor Relations.
Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in her medical testing company Theranos after making lofty promises she could not deliver.
The scandal fuelled a media circus and was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts and the biographical mini-series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.
In You Can See Everything, Fielder places himself inside the action, as in his previous projects that blur the lines between documentary, social experiment and prank show.

The film has attracted considerable interest since its trailer, showing Holmes unblinkingly asking Fielder, “Why would I deceive you?”, sparked a deluge of online memes, while a surprise debut at the Telluride Film Festival garnered rave reviews.
Deadline called the US$15 million (RM63.2 million) debut “easily the second best opening ever for a documentary at the box office after 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11”.

Third place went to Universal and Blumhouse’s Other Mommy, which collected another US$8.4 million (RM35.4 million) after topping the box office last weekend with a US$27.8 million (RM117.1 million) debut.
The horror film stars Oscar-winner Jessica Chastain in a dual role as a sinister entity terrorising a child, made even more frightening by the fact that the demon resembles the girl’s mother.
In fourth place was 20th Century’s Whalefall, a survival thriller that debuted to just US$8 million (RM33.7 million).
The movie follows a scuba diver who is swallowed by a whale and has an hour of oxygen left to escape.
“At a cost of US$60 million (RM252.9 million), the film won’t break even, even with relatively good business overseas,” Gross said.
Fifth place went to Focus Features’ new adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel Sense and Sensibility, directed by Georgia Oakley.
The film, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay, took in an estimated US$7.5 million (RM31.6 million). — AFP
Rounding out the top 10:
Verity (US$6.2 million/RM26.1 million)
Resident Evil (US$5.5 million/RM23.2 million)
Heart of the Beast (US$4.8 million/RM20.2 million)
Jailer 2 (US$3.3 million/RM13.9 million)
Forgotten Island (US$2.3 million/RM9.7 million) — AFP
85030a5a133b0c76: BEIJING: The Chinese capital Beijing is expected to become "super-aged" by 2035, with around one-third of its population aged 60 and above, the official Beijing Daily reported.

Chinese policymakers have made population planning a key part of the country's economic strategy, and this year the government faces a total potential cost of around 180 billion yuan (US$26.92 billion) to boost births, according to Reuters estimates.
One in every three residents of the Chinese capital will be aged 60 or above by 2035, the Beijing Daily reported on Saturday.
Beijing had 5.29 million permanent residents aged 60 and above at the end of last year, almost one-quarter of its population, the newspaper said.
The city's government is stepping up support for elderly residents, including raising the basic pension, the report added.

China's population has been shrinking since 2022 and is ageing rapidly, complicating government plans to boost domestic consumption and rein in debt, with hundreds of millions of people set to leave the workforce at a time when pension budgets are already stretched.
Demographers and economists argue that fewer children today could mean fewer households and slower consumption growth over time.
cbb0c5c1605d75e4: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — Zetrix AI Bhd has withdrawn its first interim dividend of 0.25 sen per share for the financial year ending Dec 31, 2026 (FY2026), declared on Aug 24, 2026.

In a filing with Bursa Malaysia today, the digital services company, formerly known as MyEG Services Bhd, said the board's decision was intended to preserve working capital following unexpected operational expenses.
The company said it would make further announcements on any material developments, as and when appropriate.
In a separate filing, Zetrix AI said trading in its securities was halted at 9 am today following the announcement and was scheduled to resume at 10 am today.
Its shares closed at 5.5 sen last Friday. — Bernama
34fba57d2070bd1e: YEREVAN: Nearly 200 nations are gathering in Armenia on Monday for critical negotiations as governments come under pressure to salvage a landmark nature pact whose goals are slipping out of reach.
Most countries joined a historic call four years ago to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 but governments have been slow to act on these pledges.
Many goals of the so-called "Paris Agreement for Nature" are falling behind, including a centrepiece commitment to protect 30% of Earth's land and oceans.
Some of the toughest objectives of the pact, such as cutting subsidies for fossil fuels and other powerful industries, have made little progress.
"We must honestly admit that collectively, we are not yet on track as needed," Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said Friday ahead of the formal UN negotiations known as COP17.
The summit comes at a difficult time, with public finances under strain and political attention fixed on conflicts, geopolitical tensions and a global energy crisis.
Only a handful of world leaders, including UN chief Antonio Guterres but mostly heads of state from nearby Central Asian nations, turned up for a high-level session ahead of the formal negotiations.
But the stakes could not be higher, Guterres said at the event on Friday, describing an unrelenting "war on nature" that threatened the very livability of the planet for future generations.
"We need more action, more speed and more will," he said.
"Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability. It is time to ask ourselves -- are we doing enough?"
A United Nations scorecard issued ahead of COP17 reported that progress toward the 23 biodiversity targets was being made -- but unevenly, and not at pace to meet the 2030 deadline.
A major tension at the summit will be money, with the report finding that the effort to close a yawning gap in necessary finance "falls far short" of what is needed.
European and other wealthy nations obligated to provide biodiversity finance have been pushing for large emerging economies like China to also contribute.
But attention is likely to focus more on how private capital, not public finances, might help plug the shortfall.
A key priority will be encouraging corporations to donate a share of profits to a near-empty UN fund to support conservation in developing countries.
Guterres also fixed the spotlight on state incentives for extractive industries, scolding governments for "spending money on the wrong things" despite pledging to reform harmful subsidies.
"Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide," said Guterres of the coal, oil and gas that are "boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity".
For the mountainous Caucasus nation of Armenia, the summit is one of the largest international events it has ever hosted, with thousands of visitors expected over the next two weeks.
The hosts have stressed that action -- not new pledges -- would define success at COP17.
"The world does not need a new vision. We have one. What it needs is delivery," Adil Najam, global president of WWF International, said Friday.
ac8288a0fe46a12e: MADRID, Oct 19 — Kylian Mbappe scored twice, including one brilliant individual goal, as Real Madrid thrashed Sevilla 4-1 yesterday to climb to third in La Liga.

Arda Guler, who was fortunate to avoid an early red card for an elbow, netted a spectacular opener before Mbappe's double and a rocket from Yan Diomande as Jose Mourinho's side moved above Real Betis.
Mbappe's first was a sensational strike involving a roulette on the edge of Sevilla's box, while his second was a chipped Panenka penalty.
Champions Barcelona are six points ahead of Real Madrid before next weekend's Clasico at Camp Nou after thrashing Betis on Saturday, with Atletico Madrid second, sandwiched between Spain's giants.
“We played a great game... we are a team and we work to improve, we've only been together for a very short time,” Mourinho told Real Madrid TV.
“It's hard to have the calm that other coaches enjoy at other clubs, given the scale of Real Madrid, but we're making the most of every minute we have.”
Mourinho lined up with Diomande on the left in place of suspended Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior and brought Guler in as part of the midfield pivot.
Vinicius's red card for hair-pulling last weekend provoked anger in the Spanish capital over officiating in Spain.

Madrid fans at the Santiago Bernabeu chanted and held up banners against La Liga president Javier Tebas after he said the club's strategy of trying to discredit referees was similar to the techniques of Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.

Los Blancos and their new coach Mourinho have complained bitterly about Spanish refereeing in recent weeks and, more generally, over the past two seasons, during which they have failed to win a major trophy.
On this occasion, it was Sevilla who had more to complain about regarding officiating as Madrid eased to victory.
A quiet start was disrupted when Madrid midfielder Guler appeared to elbow Sevilla's Peque, an incident that went unpunished midway through the first half.
“There's a match that's 11 against 11 where they deserve to win, without any doubt, but we were denied the chance to play another match,” said upset Sevilla coach Luis Garcia Plaza.
“We were denied the chance to play a match of 11 against 10. From there on I don't want to talk about the match anymore. We should have been playing 11 against 10 from the 25th minute.”
The coach said “maybe” Guler was not dismissed so Madrid did “not arrive nine points behind” Barcelona at next weekend's Clasico.
Mourinho said he had seen no replays of the incident to prove Guler had elbowed Peque.
Sevilla had resisted the probing of Madrid's attacking stars early on but were undone by a moment of magic from Guler himself after 30 minutes.
Jude Bellingham played the ball out to the flank, where record signing Diomande received it and fed Guler on the edge of the box.
The Turkish playmaker lofted a superb strike over Sevilla goalkeeper Odysseas Vlachodimos and into the top corner.
Mbappe skill
Mbappe came close to adding a second with a lightning-quick burst down the pitch, but his low effort was saved.
The French superstar soon got his goal, one of the best of the season.
Bellingham backheeled the ball into Mbappe's path and the forward produced a dazzling roulette turn into the area before showing more skill to rapidly sidestep the goalkeeper and roll the ball home.
Sevilla complained that striker Robbie Ure had been fouled in the build-up, to no avail.
Mbappe extended the lead from the penalty spot after going down under a light touch from Andres Castrin in the area.
The forward, who hopes to be crowned the world's best player at the Ballon d'Or ceremony later in October, dinked home his ninth league goal of the season.
Sevilla pulled one back with a neat strike from Manuel Bueno, but there was no fightback.
Ivorian winger Diomande thumped home from outside the box for his second goal since joining this summer from RB Leipzig, Madrid's next opponents in the Champions League.
Earlier, Real Sociedad rose to fifth with a thumping 5-2 win at bottom side Malaga, Celta Vigo defeated Alaves 2-1 and Osasuna beat Racing Santander 2-0. — AFP
71e7dcc746e3c942: KLANG: Political influencer Wan Azri Wan Deris has been cleared by the sessions court here of making a seditious statement against the government.
Judge Siti Aminah Ghazali, in a brief ruling, held that the prosecution failed to prove the charge against Azri under Section 4(1) of the Sedition Act beyond reasonable doubt.
The court also ordered the return of his RM7,000 bail.

Wan Azri, known as Papagomo, was charged with saying that the government is "pro-Israel and pro-Western (countries)" through Facebook account "Halid Hamidi (Halid Mat Kool)" at about 1pm on Nov 8, 2023.
Wan Azri was represented by lawyer Rafique Rashid Ali, while deputy public prosecutor Mustaffa P Kunyalam and Nadia Izhar appeared for the prosecution.
He was initially acquitted by the sessions court last year, but the High Court ordered him to enter defence this year following an appeal by the prosecution.
752c28460c6c49cc: IPOH, Oct 19 — More than 25,000 people from across the country have visited the grave of the late Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali in the three weeks since her passing, in a show of respect for her service and contributions.

Datuk Seri Mukhriz Mahathir, who is also her son, told Sinar Harian (SH), that the turnout was unprecedented, with mourners travelling not only from across Malaysia but also from Palembang, Indonesia, despite never having met her personally.
“I was informed that 25,000 people came from all over. This is truly a phenomenon, as they said such a situation has never happened before.
“Each time we brought my father, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad, to the grave, seeing so many people there helped ease his grief at losing his partner of 70 years,” he was quoted as saying.
Mukhriz was speaking in his capacity as Parti Pejuang Tanah Air (Pejuang) president after officiating the party’s Perak state annual convention at Hotel Seri Malaysia here, yesterday.

He recalled conversations with visitors who said they felt compelled to pay their respects because they remembered his mother’s lifelong service and struggle. Some even took leave from work simply to visit her grave, recite surah yasin, perform tahlil prayers and offer blessings.

Mukhriz said the outpouring of respect reflected the enduring legacy of Tun Dr Siti Hasmah, who served tirelessly as a doctor, particularly for rural communities, and whose contributions continue to be cherished today.
a12e66c5f0540238: BEIJING: China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers for delivering more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target.

The third-quarter gross domestic product growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday, beat the forecast for 4.4% growth in a Reuters poll, and improved from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3% in the April-to-June period.
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.

China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.
For January-September, the economy grew 4.6%, within the range of the government's annual growth target of 4.5%-5.0%.
On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2% in the third quarter, surpassing expectation for a 1.1% rise and accelerating from 0.9% in April-June.

China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of US$1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners.
A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.

Beijing has recently expanded support ‌for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors including infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan (US$82.28 billion) in unused ​government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment.

Authorities also stepped up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800 billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment.
Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2% in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in January-to-August period.
Retail sales grew 1.1% in September, improving from the 0.4% rise in August and compared with an expected 0.6% rise. It marked the quickest growth since March.
Property investment fell 20.6% in the first nine months in September.
Policymakers refrained from releasing large-scale stimulus, as strong goods exports, aided by a global AI-fuelled tech boom, should help the country to reach its annual growth target.
Industrial output expanded 5.5% in September, accelerating from the 5.2% growth in August and was in line with expectations. It marked the quickest growth in six months.
b818a0a2a6ee434d: OCTOBER 19 — Recent protests in several European countries have drawn attention to the economic and social concerns shaping people's everyday lives. Demonstrations reported on 17 October 2026 in France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal highlighted different grievances, ranging from rising living costs and housing affordability to education and public services. While some gatherings remained peaceful, others escalated into confrontations, looting and damage to property. These developments deserve careful consideration, without assuming that every protest shares the same causes or represents the views of an entire population.

France experienced particularly widespread demonstrations, with concerns about living costs and public services intersecting with student grievances over school conditions and education funding. In Belgium, student groups raised concerns about education costs and reforms affecting access to higher education. Meanwhile, demonstrations in Portugal focused heavily on housing affordability, wages and the rising cost of living. In Italy, protests over economic pressures also saw clashes in some locations. Although these events occurred within a similar period, their circumstances and demands differed.

Understanding these developments requires more than examining scenes of unrest. It also requires attention to the underlying concerns, the circumstances in which people express them and the consequences for communities.
Economic pressure and everyday decisions

From a consumer behaviour perspective, economic pressure involves more than changes in prices or income. It also shapes how individuals perceive their financial security, prioritise essential spending and plan for the future.

When a substantial proportion of household income is allocated to food, housing, transport and education, families may have less capacity to save, manage unexpected expenses or spend on other needs. Over time, these pressures can influence purchasing decisions, consumption patterns and overall wellbeing.

Housing affordability illustrates this challenge particularly clearly. When rents and property prices rise faster than incomes, households may need to reconsider where they live, how much they spend on other necessities and whether they can maintain financial stability. For younger adults, the cost of housing may also affect decisions about employment, further education and independent living.

Nevertheless, economic pressure should not be treated as a direct or universal explanation for public unrest. People respond to difficult circumstances in different ways. Their responses may be influenced by social conditions, personal experiences, confidence in public institutions and opportunities to express their concerns. Understanding the relationship between economic conditions and public demonstrations therefore requires evidence, context and careful interpretation.
Education, opportunity and future expectations

Education is another important dimension of public wellbeing. For younger generations, access to education represents not only the opportunity to gain qualifications but also the prospect of securing employment, improving their living standards and achieving greater independence.

Concerns about education funding, school conditions and the affordability of higher education can therefore extend beyond the classroom. They may reflect broader questions about equal opportunity and the extent to which individuals believe they can build a secure future through education and employment.

However, it would be inaccurate to assume that all young people share the same concerns or that student demonstrations represent the views of every member of their generation. Public opinion is diverse, and the demands raised by particular groups should be understood within their specific circumstances.

Listening to these concerns does not require agreement with every demand. Rather, it provides an opportunity to understand how people assess their prospects and what they consider necessary to improve their circumstances.
The importance of distinguishing protest from violence

Public demonstrations are a means through which people communicate their concerns and seek attention for issues they consider important. At the same time, peaceful expression must be distinguished from acts involving violence, looting, arson and damage to property.

Such actions can impose costs on people who have little or no involvement in the disputes. Small businesses may lose income, employees may be unable to work normally, and residents may experience disruption to transport, public facilities and everyday activities. Damage to public and private property can also divert resources towards repairs and recovery.

Responsible discussion must therefore recognise both the concerns expressed by demonstrators and the consequences of violence. Treating every participant as responsible for the actions of a smaller group risks overlooking the diversity of views within a demonstration. Equally, recognising public grievances does not justify actions that threaten safety or damage property.

A balanced understanding requires attention to the specific events, the conduct of those involved and the responses of the relevant authorities. This approach allows legitimate concerns to be examined without excusing harmful behaviour or making generalisations about entire communities.
What can Malaysia learn?

Developments in Europe provide an opportunity for reflection, rather than a basis for direct comparisons with Malaysia. Each country has its own economic structure, public institutions, social conditions and policy priorities. The circumstances surrounding demonstrations in Europe should not automatically be treated as evidence that Malaysia faces the same challenges or is likely to experience similar events.

Nevertheless, several broader lessons remain relevant. Understanding household experiences is essential when assessing economic wellbeing. National indicators can provide valuable information, but they may not fully capture the pressures faced by individual families, particularly when essential expenses consume an increasing share of their income.

Reliable information on household earnings, housing affordability, living costs and access to education can contribute to more informed public discussion. Such evidence can also help identify groups experiencing greater financial pressure and clarify where support may be most needed.

Communication is equally important. Public policies are more readily understood when their objectives, implications and available support measures are explained clearly. Feedback from households, workers, consumers and communities can help decision-makers identify difficulties that may not be immediately apparent in aggregate statistics.

These efforts should not be understood solely as responses to public demonstrations. They are part of the broader work required to strengthen public understanding, improve policy responsiveness and support social wellbeing.
Responsible reporting in an age of rapid information

The way public unrest is reported also influences how people understand it. Images and videos circulating online may capture dramatic incidents without providing the wider context, the sequence of events or the different perspectives of those involved.

When information is shared before it has been verified, isolated incidents can be mistaken for the overall character of a demonstration. Unverified claims may also intensify public anxiety or encourage unfair judgements about particular groups.

The media and the public therefore have an important role in distinguishing confirmed facts from speculation. Reporting should explain what is known, acknowledge what remains uncertain and avoid presenting an individual incident as representative of an entire country or population.

This responsibility is particularly important when developments occur across several countries at the same time. Similar concerns may emerge in different places, but this does not necessarily mean that the demonstrations are coordinated or driven by identical motivations.
Understanding concerns without deepening divisions

Understanding public protests does not mean endorsing every demand or excusing violence. It means examining the available evidence, recognising the complexity of social concerns and considering constructive ways to address them.

The recent developments in Europe demonstrate why public unrest should be approached with both sensitivity and analytical care. Economic pressures, education concerns and housing difficulties can affect people's sense of security, but their significance must be assessed within the circumstances of each country.

For Malaysia, the wider lesson is the importance of understanding how economic and social conditions affect everyday life. Constructive dialogue, reliable information and clear communication can help ensure that public concerns are examined without unnecessary polarisation.

Ultimately, social stability depends on more than responding when tensions arise. It also requires sustained attention to people's needs, confidence in public institutions and a willingness to engage with differing perspectives. By approaching public concerns with evidence, empathy and accountability, societies can encourage meaningful discussion without deepening divisions.

*Nurul Fardini Zakaria is a Senior Lecturer in Marketing at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), with expertise in consumer behaviour, digital marketing, sustainable consumption and consumer welfare.

affd0470220e88d3: OCTOBER 19 — A student asked prominent political leaders about corruption, 1MDB and public donations to help former prime minister Najib Razak pay a RM50 million fine. The exchange went viral, and drew extensive responses from the public including the politicians. Yes, there is something encouraging about that attention, but it is also something deeply sad. When did asking the questions universities are supposed to encourage become extraordinary enough to make headlines and go viral?
A Universiti Malaya (UM) student raised the issue at the Higher Education Ministry-backed iFUTURE dialogue.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A Universiti Malaya (UM) student raised the issue at the Higher Education Ministry-backed iFUTURE dialogue. — Picture by Firdaus Latif

The student challenged the fundraising for Najib, referred to the Tabung Haji controversy and asked how future leaders could confront corruption and feudalism with critical thinking, facts and evidence. The questions were direct, certainly. More importantly, the question demonstrated a refusal to treat political authority as a reason to avoid an uncomfortable subject.

The intervention drew extensive coverage from the news outlets and over the social media. Khairy Jamaluddin praised the student and said wrongdoing should never be defended. Selangor Menteri Besar Amirudin Shari welcomed the concern young people showed about corruption.

Johor Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi described corruption as a cancer, while warning against selective prosecution. The irony is difficult to ignore. We have grown so accustomed to silence on our campuses that a student asking difficult questions has become national news, even though this is precisely what universities are supposed to encourage.

As someone who teaches at UM, I welcome this student’s intervention. But at the same time, I also find the reaction unsettling. We teach critical thinking, ask students to interrogate evidence and encourage them to challenge established assumptions. These are principles that universities constantly emphasise as part of higher education.

Yet when a student puts them into practice by questioning political leaders on corruption, the response is one of extraordinary admiration and surprise. The student certainly deserves recognition for having the courage to speak up. But it is worth asking why exercising that courage in a university setting should still be seen as something so exceptional.

Of course, one viral video cannot prove that campuses have fallen silent. Student groups continue to organise, protest and challenge authorities, often without recognition. But as I have repeatedly argued in my commentaries on the subject of academic freedom, silence on our campuses takes many forms. It is cultivated through administrative procedures, hierarchies and the expectation that difficult subjects should be handled carefully.

A forum needs approval, an invitation becomes a negotiation, and students learn which discussions might cause trouble. Lecturers, too, know the temptation to avoid controversy. Over time, people begin to censor themselves long before anyone issues an instruction.

In April this year, UM student groups alleged that an integrity and anti-corruption forum was disrupted when access to its planned venue was blocked. It is reported that university authorities required prior approval for campus forums, citing procedures and harmony, while student organisers said obtaining approval was often difficult. There is a disturbing contrast between celebrating an anti-corruption question at a ministry-backed event and the difficulties students have reported in organising anti-corruption discussions on campus.

Deputy Higher Education Minister Adam Adli Abdul Halim has since defended the student’s remarks as fair comment, while several politicians voiced support. UM vice-chancellor Noor Azuan Abu Osman confirmed on 17 October that no disciplinary action had been taken against the student and affirmed that differences of opinion should be heard.

These assurances are welcome. But freedom should be demonstrated in everyday campus practices, especially when students challenge those currently exercising power, including university administrators themselves.

Even more troubling is the harassment that followed. The student reported that personal photographs from social media were taken without consent, alongside attacks on physical appearance and threats of expulsion.

People may disagree with the student’s language or political views. They have every right to argue back. But personal attacks and intimidation have consequences beyond this particular incident. They send a chilling message to other students that speaking up may come at a considerable personal cost.

The student’s experience also raises important questions about the ongoing efforts to repeal the Universities and University Colleges Act (UUCA), particularly whether legal reform alone can guarantee students the freedom to speak, question and challenge authority.

In August, the Higher Education Ministry directed public universities to stop disciplinary proceedings over student expression, public criticism and peaceful assembly. This is an important commitment, but changing legislation cannot by itself eliminate habits of caution and deference. Genuine academic freedom must also extend to student-organised forums, invited speakers, political disagreements and questions that university leaders would rather avoid.

This requires clear institutional safeguards, accessible complaint mechanisms and independent oversight to ensure that students can exercise these freedoms without facing harassment or disciplinary retaliation.

We should also expect more from the politicians who applauded the student. Saying corruption is wrong is easy. The harder task is to demonstrate consistency when allegations implicate allies, institutions or political patrons. The questions deserved substantive answers about the political culture that continues to excuse wrongdoing, rather than admiration for the boldness of asking them.

I hope this student’s willingness to speak encourages others. More importantly, I hope we will reach a point where students can ask difficult questions in lecture theatres and public forums, engage in open disagreements without fear of threats, and return to their studies without worrying about the consequences of speaking up.
The health of our universities should be measured by how much space we give students to think independently, question authority and express themselves freely.
Until then, we should celebrate the courage to speak while being much less comfortable with the silence that made it newsworthy.
*Khoo Ying Hooi, PhD is associate professor at Universiti Malaya. She is also co-founder and advisor of Southeast Asia Coalition on Academic Freedom (SEACAF).
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
402afd9677c02844: SINGAPORE, Oct 19 — When Carrie Wong first heard she would be starring alongside South Korean actor Lee Joon-gi in the new international drama thriller Kidnap Game, sleep became the last thing on her mind.
The 32-year-old local actress told AsiaOne recently that she was in London when her manager called her at around 3am to share the news.
“I was already having trouble sleeping because of the time difference,” Carrie recalled with a laugh. “Then my manager called... and I was like, ‘Wow, I’m so excited!’ then I couldn’t sleep already.”
While details about the project and the script were not yet finalised at the time, she said she was immediately drawn to the thriller concept.
“Being part of (a thriller series) is something I’ve never thought of before, but it was very exciting,” she said.

Kidnap Game is a suspense thriller series that centres around seven simultaneous kidnappings across Asia, with the victims’ families becoming entangled in a deadly game. Each character is assigned a vastly different mission in a scheme designed to claim six lives, leaving only one survivor.

Carrie plays cheerful flight attendant Janice whose fiance, played by local actor Herman Keh, is kidnapped. Meanwhile, Joon-gi, 44, plays genius surgeon Han Ki-joo, whose visually impaired daughter is kidnapped.

The series also stars Japanese actor Kentaro Sakaguchi as elite detective Toshiro Niide, Taiwanese actress Alice Ko as influencer housewife Christina, Filipino actor Joel Torre as taxi driver Miguel, Thai actress Praew Narupornkamol Chaisang as nightclub hostess Ayun, and Stanley Yau – a member of Hong Kong’s popular boy group Mirror – as multinational corporate lawyer Andy.

It is produced by Hong Kong-based MakerVille, in collaboration with South Korean production company SimStory and Japan’s Fuji Television, and was also filmed in Hong Kong, Taipei, Seoul, Tokyo, Bangkok, Manila and Okinawa.
On whether she needed convincing to join the series, Carrie candidly admitted that she didn’t even need to see the script.
“I’ll definitely do it because of course I want to work with Joon-gi and Kentaro,” she laughed, adding that the opportunity to be part of a regional production was another major draw.
She was also especially intrigued by the show’s premise.
While most thriller series such as Squid Game and Alice in Borderland see the characters compete for their own survival, Kidnap Game is about fighting to save your loved ones, she explained.

“I’ve never seen this kind of concept before. Usually when you take part in a survival game, if you lose, you die. But this one is very different. I think this is worse,” she said. “I just feel like this is very brutal.”
Initial impression of Joon-gi
Carrie filmed all her scenes in Singapore and Joon-gi was the only cast member whom she worked with in person during production.
Although there were scenes featuring her and some cast members, Carrie never got the chance to film with them in person.
Carrie and Joon-gi were spotted filming together near Merlion Park and at the Bayfront area in November last year.

The latter was also spotted shooting solo scenes at Joo Chiat and previously shared an Instagram post featuring photos and videos of himself viewing Christmas decorations at Orchard Road and jogging from Clarke Quay to Marina Bay.

Despite her excitement about working with Joon-gi, Carrie admitted that her initial impression of the Korean star came from his role in the 2016 historical K-drama Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo, where he stars as fourth prince Wang So.
She described his character as “so stern and so scary”, which shaped her first impression of him. However, that image quickly disappeared once they began filming.
She revealed that Joon-gi’s actual personality is “a complete contrast”, describing him as very cheerful, bubbly and extroverted.
Beyond his warm personality, Carrie was also thoroughly impressed by his language skills, revealing that he spoke fluent Japanese on set despite having a translator.

On how the two of them built their chemistry and rapport on set, Carrie noted that there was little pressure to develop their relationship as their characters are strangers from different regions of the world forced into the same situation.
She added that they would simply go with the flow on set and that everything was open for discussion.
Because of the story’s intense plot and heavy theme, most of their off-camera moments were spent unwinding.
“There’s nothing happy about the entire series,” Carrie quipped. “Other than some happy flashback scenes, it’s quite tiring.”
And while she knows some Korean and was able to communicate a little with Joon-gi in it, she couldn’t go into anything deeper without help.
“Everything I needed to communicate on set was too difficult for me to express in Korean,” she said.
The two would instead spend their downtime resting and having casual conversations between takes.
Carrie even attempted to teach Joon-gi the meanings of some Singlish words such as lah, leh, and lor, which she quickly realised were “very difficult to explain”.
Meeting the rest of the cast
Carrie recently attended the drama’s premiere in Tokyo, where she finally had the chance to meet the rest of the international cast.
She admitted that she felt a sense of familiarity seeing Alice in particular: “When everyone around you is speaking Japanese or Korean, it’s nice having someone you can speak Chinese with.”
She added that one of the most amusing parts of the premiere was watching translators juggle multiple languages throughout the press conference.
She said: “I’ve never seen translators so busy before.”
She told us she wished she had been able to film scenes with the other cast members, but nonetheless, some of the cast members have kept in touch since then.
She said she had plans to catch up with Joel, who was in Singapore until Oct 15.
Carrie also revealed a second season of Kidnap Game may already be in the pipeline. — AsiaOne
9127221793dbfa0a: NOTTINGHAM, Oct 19 — Mikel Arteta said Arsenal’s strength in depth will be key to their Premier League title defence after Noni Madueke came off the bench to clinch a 1-0 win against Nottingham Forest yesterday.
Arteta’s side were well below their best at the City Ground and did not register a shot on target until Madueke bagged their winner 10 minutes from full-time.
While the Gunners earned few style points in the East Midlands, they will not be overly concerned after moving within three points of leaders Manchester City.
Arteta is able to dip into one of the stronger substitutes’ benches in the top flight and he made full use of the resources at his disposal to turn the tide by the banks of the River Trent.
Crucially, he sent on Madueke for the underwhelming Eberechi Eze at half-time.
He also introduced Mikel Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Jurrien Timber as the second half wore on.
It was Madueke who provided the key intervention, cutting in from the left flank to unleash a powerful drive that deflected past Forest goalkeeper Matz Sels in the 80th minute.
“We had to earn it until the last second. They are a well-coached team and hard to break down. We had to take risks, they are a dangerous team,” Arteta said.
“We had to manage the emotional part really well. We stayed focused and the finishers made a huge impact.”
Arsenal are in the midst of a hectic schedule which included a Champions League win over Lille in midweek and a looming European trip to Bayern Munich on Wednesday.
Arteta’s ability to rest key players without significantly weakening his team could be a major factor in the title race.
“Some of them played three days ago and some of them will start the next game and they know that everyone has to be at it,” he said.
“If you are needed after 60 minutes, 45 minutes and sometimes two minutes. We have a squad now that can deliver in moments and we have to use that.
“Noni, Jurrien, Mikel was brilliant when he came on and Viktor really changed the game, all of them did and that’s what we need.
“Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that’s the difference.”
After a shock 3-0 loss at Brighton on September 19, second-placed Arsenal have bounced back with three successive victories.
The north Londoners have not been able to recapture the relentless consistency that took them to a first title in 22 years last season.
But they retain the priceless ability to grind out wins and this was their sixth in seven league matches.
“Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn’t have a shot on target and that’s something we discussed,” Arteta said.
“We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it’s in.” — AFP

b15e79f3c5b1422c: London, Oct 19 — Michael Carrick said Manchester United’s hard-fought 1-1 draw at bitter rivals Leeds yesterday felt like a “fresh start” even though their long wait for a win goes on.
Leeds forward Dominic Calvert-Lewin cancelled out Bryan Mbeumo’s first-half opener at Elland Road, extending United’s winless run to six matches in all competitions.
But Carrick saw positive signs five days after the 2-0 Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid, which sparked Lisandro Martinez’s criticism of the club hierarchy over a lack of summer investment.
“We’re not getting too carried away because we haven’t won the game,” said the Red Devils boss, who started the Argentina defender at Leeds but had to replace him at the break due to a thigh problem.
“I think if you keep doing the right things for the right reasons then you get what you deserve in the end.
“It felt like a bit of a fresh start, if I’m honest, today in where we’re at and accepting it and doing something about it.

“It definitely shows that the boys are desperate to do well for each other as much as anything else and how much they appreciate playing for this football club, because there was a real purpose to the group over the last couple of days.”

United head to Como on Wednesday looking for a first victory since last month’s Champions League opener against Sabah before attempting to kick-start their Premier League campaign at home to Bournemouth.
The Red Devils, in 13th spot, have their fewest wins at this stage of a top-flight campaign since 1986-87.
“We’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch,” said the under-pressure Carrick. “I’m realistic with that.
“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of where you have to find a way through it.”
He added: “I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve got no doubts that we can go on a good run.” — AFP
2c76cc087c448162: Hari ini Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim dijadual mempengerusikan apa yang dipanggil mesyuarat Jawatankuasa Peringkat Tertinggi Pengurusan Bencana Pusat. Mesyuarat akan bincang isu berkaitan jerebu (obviously) termasuk penyelarasan tindakan antara kementerian. Harapan saya apa jua keputusan yang dicapai akan dilaksanakan dengan efficient. Tidak ada tunggu-tunggu, tidak ada lengah-lengah, tidak ada tidak tahu siapa buat apa. Mesyuarat juga akan membincangkan perkembangan kebakaran di Indonesia. Sekali lagi saya kata obviously. Yes it all about dollars and cents. Maka apilah solusinya bagi syarikat termasuk yang bertaraf 'gergasi' serta tuan punya ladang. Cari mereka yang terlibat dan ambil tindakan? Sudah dibuat dahulu. Jadi mengapa kebakaran berulang saban tahun?
Mungkin tindakan tidak menyeluruh. Mungkin ada syarikat terlepas. Mungkin undang-undang tidak ketat dan denda tidak tinggi. Tidak setimpal dengan apa yang dilakukan. Semuanya kemungkinan.

Kali ini Singapura sudah hantar notis langkah pencegahan kepada tujuh syarikat di Indonesia yang dikaitkan dengan kebakaran hutan dan tanah gambut sehingga menyebabkan jerebu rentas sempadan yang parah. Kata kuncinya ialah 'syarikat di Indonesia'. Oleh itu, mungkin syarikat berpangkalan atau beroperasi di Indonesia tetapi tidak semestinya Indonesian, sebaliknya milik negara asing? Mungkin pemegang konsesi warga Malaysia atau Singapura? 'Syarikat di Indonesia' tentu sahaja boleh juga milik warga Indonesia.

Singapura tidak tolak kemungkinan untuk mengenakan penalti kewangan dan tindakan undang-undang jenayah jika tujuh syarikat yang ia namakan gagal mematuhi notis. Jurucakap Kerajaan Malaysia, Fahmi Fadzil, pula berkata tiada syarikat perladangan Malaysia dikenal pasti terbabit dalam aktiviti pembakaran di Indonesia yang mencetuskan jerebu.
Alhamdulillah, baguslah begitu tetapi 'tiada dikenal pasti' bukan jaminan 100% syarikat kita tidak terbabit. This can only mean they have not been located and identified. I hope this is not the case.

Sama ada syarikat kita terlibat atau tidak, realitinya kita terkesan teruk dengan jerebu. Bak kata Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman, Malaysia mesti bersedia ambil tindakan ke atas syarikatnya jika ada yang terlibat. Beliau mahu bantahan diplomatik Asean diselaraskan serta sekatan pembiayaan terhadap syarikat yang dikaitkan dengan amalan pembakaran terbuka. Kata beliau, bank-bank utama serantau boleh beri tekanan dengan menghentikan pembiayaan kepada syarikat yang didapati terbabit -- syarikat yang walaupun sedikit terkait dengan slash-and-burn tactics ini mesti disekat dan tidak boleh dapat lagi akses modal pasaran dan akses pinjaman, bukan setakat di Malaysia dan Singapura.

Ertinya beliau sarankan cut their access and hurt their wallet. Hurt them where it hurts them most, kata Syed Saddiq. Betul dan mungkin kita akan dapat atasi masalah kebakaran tahunan sekali gus jerebu once and for all.
